source.title: Beyond Implicit Bias: The Insignificance of SGD Noise in Online Learning
source.authors: Nikhil Vyas; Depen Morwani; Rosie Zhao; Gal Kaplun; S. Kakade; B. Barak

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares batch sizes and reports held-out performance in online and offline training, bearing on V5's batch-size claim. It does not use the fixed-epoch comparison specified in that version.
record.gate_note: The paper measures online/offline held-out performance as batch size varies, and reports an explicit weight-decay comparison. It does not test random-label memorization, width, dropout, adaptive-optimizer generalization, or sharpness. Results cited from prior work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: Figure 10 directly tests V5 by comparing test error at equal numbers of examples processed, equivalent to equal epoch budgets within each fixed dataset. The main equal-step comparisons do not establish the fixed-epoch effect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors find no implicit-bias benefit from small-batch noise in their online settings, while offline noise can improve eventual performance. They support a common online trajectory in loss and function space. Their computational interpretation is compatible with Figure 10's small-batch advantage at equal samples processed.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares batch-size effects and online versus offline training; it does not test the original claim's fixed-epoch generalization-gap protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported batch-size effect differs between online and offline regimes. Figure 10 also compares trends by samples seen, but its prose does not specify their direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches improve online performance per gradient step on CIFAR-5m, ImageNet and C4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these online settings, larger batches improve optimization progress per update; this does not imply an advantage at equal data budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay improves online CIFAR-5m test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit weight decay can improve online learning performance even where small-batch noise provides no implicit-bias advantage.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The paper does not report train-test gaps for the batch-size comparisons. Its main comparisons are by gradient steps, not a fixed epoch budget. Exact values for the cited comparisons are figure-only; the prose gives qualitative directions. The authors note that further research may be needed to understand generalizability beyond the three datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Figure 4 and Figures 6, 11, 13–15 test loss-trajectory or function-space similarity after changing batch size, not the held-out performance comparison named in V5.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization using the same architectures and recipes.
Generalization as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Fixed-epoch comparisons for ImageNet and C4; systematic batch-size thresholds; recovery through longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, or normalization and regularization changes.
Dropout effects, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlations with generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Offline ConvNext-T/ImageNet batch-size comparison is omitted. Figure 3(b) includes offline curves, and the text reports an eventual higher-noise advantage. Record it separately with the equal-step budget limitation.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's online challenges verdicts: equal-step advantages do not reverse a fixed-epoch claim. Figure 10 supplies the relevant matched-data comparison, and its direction is explicitly stated in the supplied text. Exact effect sizes are unavailable from the extracted plots.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under tuning.
Fixed epoch budgets and workload-dependent batch-size thresholds; the reported primary comparisons use training steps.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train-test gaps.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared batch sizes in online CIFAR-5m training; measured test error against training steps.
rows.value: Lower-noise runs consistently outperform higher-noise runs per given step.
rows.uncertainty: Experiments averaged over ≥ 4 runs; error bars shown in Figure 8.
rows.note: The text gives the direction of the comparison, not exact test-error values.
rows.check: Larger batches perform better per gradient step, but process more examples per step. This cannot establish a reversal of V5's fixed-epoch penalty.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared batch sizes by number of samples seen in online and offline CIFAR-5m training.
rows.value: The trend with number of examples remains similar in offline and online regimes.
rows.note: The paper states the trend but does not specify the direction or exact values in the prose.
rows.check: The extraction missed Appendix E.1's explicit statement that larger batches perform worse when indexed by samples seen. Equal samples imply equal epochs within each regime. Set the baseline to smaller batches and record higher test error for larger batches; split online and offline into separate rows.
